justification: Focused technical pass built around the four specific items flagged for this round, plus a general read for fabrication, code correctness and citation integrity. (1) Heapify empirical claim: verified the 15-node per-height accounting by hand -- 1 node at height 3 (subtotal 3), 2 nodes at height 2 (subtotal 4), 4 nodes at height 1 (subtotal 4), 8 leaves at height 0 (subtotal 0), total 11, against the naive 15x3=45 bound -- both the prose and Figure 3's <desc> state this correctly and it checks out arithmetically. The measured table itself (build/n: 1.83/1.87/1.87/1.87; insert/n: 2.14/2.20/2.21/2.24 for n=1000..8000) is the real, harness-verified output of the article's own code (`run-code.mjs` PASS), and I independently reproduced the bottom-up MinHeap build by hand on the article's own [5,3,8,1,9,2,7] example (parent=2 sifts 8 down past 2; parent=1 sifts 3 down past 1; parent=0 sifts 5 down through 1 then 3) and got [1,3,2,5,9,8,7], matching the article's stated output exactly. The worst-case-vs-measured comparison (1 + log2(8000) ~= 14 vs. measured 2.24, 'six times') is arithmetically correct. However, the paragraph does cross into exactly the overclaim the round-1 brief for this article asked me to check for: 'On uniformly random input, most insertions settle after a swap or two, nowhere near the tree's full height -- the average is far closer to the bottom-up build's flat shape than the per-insert worst case implies.' This is a specific, non-obvious claim about the *distribution* of sift-up depths on random input -- the article measured only the aggregate comparisons/n ratio, never a per-insertion swap-depth histogram, and cites no source for an average-case sift-up bound (the only cited proposition, Sedgewick & Wayne, is explicitly the worst case). It reads as an authoritative theoretical explanation for the gap rather than the plain report the round brief calls for, and it is not licensed by anything actually measured or cited in the article -- a violation of EDITORIAL_BRIEF rule 3 ('every non-obvious factual claim has a primary source') and the pilot-round lesson against 'what most people think'-style unsourced generalizations. (2) CLRS chapter-only citation: grepped binary-search-trees.md and sorting-algorithms-compared.md, both already published -- both cite CLRS by chapter number only ('CLRS, chapter 6/8/12/13', no page numbers) alongside the same mitpress.mit.edu front-matter URL, with binary-search-trees.round-1.technical.json documenting that MIT Press's page 403s automated fetches. This article's single CLRS citation ('CLRS derives the same bound with the same per-height accounting, as the running-time analysis of BUILD-MAX-HEAP (CLRS, chapter 6)') follows the identical pattern -- consistent with precedent, no issue. (3) Verified via direct fetch of dotnet/runtime's PriorityQueue.cs (raw.githubusercontent.com/dotnet/runtime/main/...) that `private const int Arity = 4;` is real and that `Heapify` builds bottom-up from an initial collection, with the source's own comments noting leaves need no correction and that this is faster than sequential enqueuing -- confirming both the Arity=4 (quaternary heap) claim and the 'source's own Heapify method' claim the article makes. (4) IndexedMinHeap/DecreaseKey: traced the full exercise program by hand, instruction by instruction, against the position map. Three pushes (backup:5, compact-index:5, send-digest:2) sift correctly via SiftUp with Swap keeping _position in sync (final state keys=[send-digest,compact-index,backup], priorities=[2,5,5]); DecreaseKey('compact-index',0) correctly looks up position 1, overwrites the priority, and SiftUp(1) swaps it to the root, again updating _position for both swapped keys. All three subsequent Pop() calls -- including MoveEntry's self-copy no-op on the final single-element pop -- reproduce the article's exact stated output (0: compact-index, 2: send-digest, 5: backup). I specifically checked the position-map-invalidation risk flagged for this item: every code path that moves an entry (Swap inside SiftUp/SiftDown, and MoveEntry inside Pop's root-replacement) updates `_position` for the moved key immediately, so no stale index survives a swap; I could not construct a scenario in this implementation where `_position[key]` goes stale. The one real gap, noted as a minor issue below, is that DecreaseKey has no guard against being called with a priority that is not actually smaller (unlike CLRS's canonical DECREASE-KEY, which includes an explicit error check) -- calling it with a larger priority would silently corrupt the heap invariant since only SiftUp runs. Also verified independently: the PriorityQueue main-class Remarks page quotes verbatim ('Implements an array-backed, quaternary min-heap...Note that the type does not guarantee first-in-first-out semantics for elements of equal priority'); the Remove method Remarks quotes verbatim ('The method performs a linear-time scan of every element in the heap, removing the first value found to match the element parameter' and 'what entry does get removed is non-deterministic and does not take priority into account'); and the Dequeue method page confirms it throws InvalidOperationException specifically 'The queue is empty' -- all match the article's inline quotes and characterizations exactly, with no clipping out of context. Cross-checked the article's description of how dijkstra-shortest-path.md works around the missing decrease-key ('leaving stale duplicates in the queue and skipping them with a visited set') against that already-published article's own code -- accurate. Checked the cross-link anchor to sorting-algorithms-compared.md ('#heap-sort-quicksorts-guarantee-built-into-the-algorithm') against that file's actual heading ('## Heap sort: quicksort's guarantee, built into the algorithm') -- slugs match. No fabricated numbers, no copied prose, no algorithm stated without its cost and conditions; every complexity claim (sift-up/down O(log n), heapify O(n), Remove O(n), top-k O(n log k), k-way merge O(n log k)) is stated with the operation and case it applies to.

issues.location: "Add decrease-key by tracking positions" exercise solution, `IndexedMinHeap<TKey,TPriority>.DecreaseKey`
issues.problem: `DecreaseKey` blindly overwrites the priority and calls `SiftUp` with no check that `newPriority` is actually smaller than the current one. If a caller passed a larger priority by mistake, `SiftUp` would silently do nothing useful (the node may need to sift down instead), leaving the heap invariant broken with no error raised. CLRS's canonical DECREASE-KEY includes an explicit 'error: new key is greater than current key' check; this implementation omits any such guard.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either add a guard (`if (_comparer.Compare(newPriority, _priorities[i]) > 0) throw new ArgumentException(...)`) and mention it in the prose, or note explicitly in the exercise text that the sketch assumes callers only ever decrease, matching the method's name.
